statement: A tin holds 7 yellow, 5 blue and 4 green crayons. In the dark, Leo takes crayons out one at a time. How many must he take to be sure of having at least two crayons of one colour and at least two crayons of another colour?

choices.misconception: I imagined the lucky case of 2 yellow and 2 blue straight away and added one spare crayon, but being sure means planning for the unluckiest order.
I imagined all 7 yellow crayons coming first and thought one more crayon would finish the job, but one blue crayon is only a single, not two.
I found the biggest unlucky handful, 7 yellow, 1 blue and 1 green, but forgot to take the one extra crayon that forces success.
I worked out how many crayons guarantee one of every colour, 7 + 5 + 1, which answers a different question.

hints: Imagine the unluckiest possible order of pencils.
Find the largest handful that still fails: at most one colour may have two or more crayons. Make that failing handful as big as possible, then one more crayon forces success.
A failing handful can hold all 7 yellow crayons but only one blue and one green, which is 9 crayons.

solutions.reliable: A handful fails when at most one colour has two or more crayons. To make a failing handful as big as possible, let the largest colour be the one with many: all 7 yellow, plus 1 blue and 1 green, which is 9 crayons and still fails. Using blue or green as the big colour gives fewer, such as 5 + 1 + 1 = 7. Any 10th crayon is blue or green and gives that colour its second crayon, so 10 crayons are always enough, and 9 are not. The transferable idea: to be sure, build the biggest set that still fails, then add one.

whyOnTest: Worst-case questions ask for the largest failing handful plus one; the traps are picturing a lucky draw or answering a different guarantee.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
